entries.name: Tithe barn
entries.purpose: storage of tithe grain and threshed harvest; wagon entrances for loaded carts
parts: double wagon doors at the gables
layout: a long timber rectangle, door on the long south side
open threshing floor in the middle bay
grain stacked in the flanking aisles
wagons enter from both ends
entries.found: one per large manor or monastery, beside the farmyard
entries.notes: The medieval farm's cathedral. Cressing Temple's Wheat Barn (built 1257-1280, about 39 m by 13 m) is a standing benchmark; expect them as landmarks the player can enter with a cart.

entries.name: Gambrel barn
materials: wood shingle or corrugated metal roof
entries.purpose: hay and grain storage above; livestock stalls or equipment below
layout: a deep gable-ended rectangle
loft accessed by a hay track on the ridge
big sliding doors on the long face
ramp or stair to the loft
entries.found: singly on farms across the American east and Midwest
entries.notes: The definitive American farm icon: the gambrel roof doubles the usable loft volume compared to a gable. Hay hoods and track beams are the tell-tale silhouette.

entries.name: Fachwerkscheune
materials: brick or wattle and daub infill
entries.purpose: mixed farm storage, livestock and harvest under one steep steep gable
layout: a rectangle with the ridge running long-ways
threshing bay in the centre, stalls or storage flanking
visible dark beam lattice on the walls
entries.found: farm clusters across central Europe, often attached to the farmhouse
entries.notes: The half-timbered look reads instantly as continental Europe: dark beams, light infill. Walls carry little of the load; removing infill panels does not collapse the barn.

entries.name: Dutch barn
entries.purpose: open-fronted hay and straw storage, machinery cover
layout: a wide open-fronted shed on a concrete pad
hay stacked in bays along the back
no doors or walls on the working face
entries.found: one or more beside every modern livestock farm
entries.notes: The cheap modern hay barn: nothing but a roof on posts. Despite the name it is a British term; vast open bays with loose hay are its identifying read.

entries.name: Livery stable
entries.purpose: housing horses: stalls, tack, feed and hay store
layout: a long range facing a yard
stalls in a row, feed passage behind
hay over the stables, winch and hatch to the loft
entries.found: in farmyards, coaching inns and market towns
entries.notes: Working stables smell of hay and horses: damp ground, flies, manure heap. The hayloft above the stalls is the point of two storeys in one building.

entries.name: Cow byre
entries.purpose: winter housing and milking of cattle
layout: one long range, doors at both ends
cows in stalls facing a central aisle
loft over the stalls
entries.found: on dairy farms, usually hard against the field gate
entries.notes: Low, dark and ammonia-rich. Byres double as status markers: the size of the cow shed told the village the farm's wealth.

entries.name: Pigsty
entries.purpose: housing pigs for meat and manure
layout: a small hovel against a wall, open to a yard
trough under cover, wallow in the sun
drain runs to the midden
entries.found: at the back of every small farmstead, downwind of the house
entries.notes: Deliberately grim and functional. In hot climates a wallow is mandatory; the trough doubles as a soap dish for anything fallen from the kitchen.

entries.name: Chicken coop
entries.purpose: housing poultry for eggs and meat
layout: a small hutch on the ground, facing away from the prevailing wind
nest boxes at the back, perch above
pop-hole opens onto a fenced run
blueprint: layer 0: w w w w w|w . . . w|w . n . w|w w d w w
layer 1: r r r r r|r r r r r
legend: w timber wall, d door, n nesting boxes, r thatch roof, . air
entries.found: in every farmyard and many cottages' gardens
entries.notes: The smallest real farm building; the kind of structure a player can build in minutes and then lose sleep over when a fox moves in.

entries.name: Sheepfold
entries.purpose: holding sheep for shearing, dipping, lambing or overnight safety
layout: a loose circle or semicircle open to windward
funnel mouth narrowing to a single file race
hurdles pen off sections for sorting
blueprint: legend: w drystone wall, s sheep in the fold, . air
entries.found: on open hillsides in pairs, one for lambing and one for shearing
entries.notes: No roof, no door, no wood: a wall is all that keeps two hundred sheep on a treeless hillside. Drystone folds last centuries untouched.

entries.name: Staddle granary
entries.purpose: rat-proof storage of threshed grain above the ground
layout: a small square hut standing on stone mushrooms about 0.7 m tall
hatch at first-floor level, reached by ladder
corn stored in bulk inside
blueprint: layer 1: f f f f f|f . . . f|f . g . f|f . . . f|f f d f f
layer 2: . r r r .|r r r r r|r r r r r
legend: s staddle stone, f oak floor and brick wall, g grain sacks, d hatch, r tile roof, . air
entries.found: singly or in pairs beside the great barn in English farmyards
entries.notes: The staddle stones are the whole idea: rats cannot climb the thin stem, and grain kept dry above the damp spoils far less. Cressing Temple's Elizabethan granary is the largest in Essex.

entries.name: Corn crib
entries.purpose: drying and storing ear corn in the husk
parts: slatted or wire-mesh walls with 2-3 cm gaps
layout: a long narrow box on piers, slatted all round so air moves through the corn
unshelled ears loaded from the top or end
shelled or fed straight down
entries.found: in pairs or rows beside the barn in the American corn belt
entries.notes: The ventilation gap is the design: corn enters wet and dries in the crib. Slatted cylinders and cribs are different species of the same animal.

entries.name: Tower silo
entries.purpose: fermenting (ensiling) green chopped fodder for winter stock feed
layout: a single tall cylinder beside the byre
filled from the top with blown chopped grass
silage drawn from the bottom through a side door
entries.found: in twos and threes beside dairy farms
entries.notes: A silo full of silage is a bomb of fermentation: the first 24 hours vent CO2. Building one taller than wide is entirely about cheaper foundations per cubic metre.

entries.name: Root cellar
entries.purpose: keeping vegetables and preserves cool and frost-free through winter without power
layout: a buried box or vaulted pit with a hatch at ground level
slots for air in and out
shelf roots on top, preserves below
entries.found: dug into a bank or hillside beside the farmhouse
entries.notes: A hole in the ground with ideas above it: at 1.5-3 m depth the soil stays near 10-12 C all year. Pre-electric fridge that only ever needed a shovel.

entries.name: Ice house
entries.purpose: keeping winter-cut pond ice frozen into summer for food preservation
layout: a domed pit with a covered shaft at the top
ice lowered on a ramp, packed in sawdust
meltwater drains away below
entries.found: on country estates and farms near stillwater ponds
entries.notes: A winter harvested, summer spent. One good ice harvest kept an estate in cold meat and fish for a year; the dome shape sheds water off the ice.

entries.name: Smokehouse
entries.purpose: smoking and preserving meat and fish with hardwood smoke
layout: a small square hut sealed from draughts
fire in the pit below, meat hung above
smoke curls up and out of the peak vent
entries.found: attached to farmhouses in pork-and-bacon country
entries.notes: A dry, cool hut and a slow fire: hams hang for weeks. The same room that preserves bacon will taint a side of salmon if the wrong wood burns.

entries.name: Dairy
entries.purpose: cooling and processing milk into butter and cheese
layout: a small north-facing room kept cold
open shelves for cream pans
stream or spring runs through or beside it
entries.found: built into the farmhouse range or as a standalone shed
entries.notes: The coolest room on the farm, often literally built over the spring. Before refrigeration, the dairy was the only room where butter survived July.

entries.name: Village bakehouse
entries.purpose: communal baking of bread for the whole village in one wood-fired oven
layout: a single-room building dominated by the oven mouth
off-centre chimney over the dome
work trough along the wall
entries.found: one per village, often beside the manor or in the market square
entries.notes: Everyone's loaf, one fire. Villages banned private ovens to save wood; a week's baking day filled the queue, and the last loaves went in as the oven cooled.

entries.name: Farmhouse brewery
entries.purpose: small-scale brewing of beer or ale for the household and estate
layout: a two-storey room with the copper on the heated lower floor
wort runs downhill into vats
cellar below for conditioning
entries.found: in big farmhouses and monasteries, sometimes beside the bakehouse
entries.notes: Farm ale was a staple food, not a luxury: weak small beer for daily drinking, strong ale for feast days. The brewhouse is the ancestor of every village pub.

entries.name: Watermill
entries.purpose: grinding grain into flour (gristmill), later driving saws and hammers
layout: a stone or timber house over the stream, wheel on the gable
leat races water onto the wheel
gearing carries power up to the stones on the first floor
entries.found: one per parish on a steady stream, often with a mill pond
entries.notes: The most consequential industrial building of the pre-steam age. A good overshot wheel delivers 5-10 hp; the miller took a toll in flour for every bag ground.

entries.name: Smock windmill
entries.purpose: grinding grain or pumping water using wind power
layout: a tall polygonal tower with a rotating cap
sails turned into the wind by tail pole or winch
stones on an upper floor, sacks hoisted by the sail spindle
entries.found: on flat, windy coasts and polders, scattered along ridges inland
entries.notes: The Dutch drained a delta with these and ground its bread too. The cap rotates to face the wind; sails reef by hand when the gale rises.

entries.name: Tide mill
entries.purpose: grinding grain with the twice-daily rhythm of the tides
layout: a barrage or wall enclosing a tidal pond
pond fills at high tide, gates shut, pond empties through wheels at low tide
mill sits on the wall or beside it
entries.found: on tidal estuaries with a decent tidal range, e.g. Eling Tide Mill in Hampshire
entries.notes: A clockwork mill: it works when the tide lets it work, roughly twice a day for a few hours. The greatest constraint in pre-steam engineering was the moon.

entries.name: Water-powered sawmill
entries.purpose: sawing logs into boards and beams
layout: an open-fronted shed straddling a mill race
wheel outside drives a vertical frame saw
logs rolled in on a carriage, boards carried out the back
entries.found: on fast forest streams, often with a log pond
entries.notes: Before the sawmill, a two-man saw pit was the technology; a water saw did a day's pit work in an hour. The sound carried downwind for miles.

entries.name: Fulling mill
entries.purpose: felting and cleaning woven cloth with pounding stocks
layout: a stone building over the stream
wheel drives hammers that bat the cloth in a trough
finished cloth stretched on hooks outside to dry
entries.found: on woollen-cloth rivers, in clusters of mills
entries.notes: One of the first industrial processes to be mechanised, because beating wet wool is brute force. Fuller's earth or stale urine supplied the cleaning chemistry.

entries.name: Charcoal clamp
entries.purpose: slow-burning wood into charcoal for smithing and cooking
layout: a dome of stacked wood over a central chimney, sealed in turf
fired from the top or side, burns for one to two weeks
kept oxygen-starved so the wood chars rather than burns
blueprint: layer 0: . t t .|t w w t|t w w t|. t t .
legend: t turf seal, w stacked cordwood, . air
entries.found: deep in managed woodland, one clearing per coppice cycle
entries.notes: The smith's fuel, made on-site where the wood grows. A clamp is tended day and night for a week; smoke rises white then blue as it cooks, and the maker sleeps beside it.

entries.name: Blacksmith's forge
entries.purpose: shoeing horses and making and repairing iron tools and fittings
layout: an open-fronted shop so the smith works in daylight
forge to one side, anvil under the open wall
hoof parings and sweepings swept to the back
entries.found: one per village, usually on the main street near the inn
entries.notes: The village specialist: horseshoe, ploughshare, gate hinge, nail. Sparks, ringing and the smell of hot sulphur; the door stands open all day.

entries.name: Carpenter's workshop
entries.purpose: making and repairing timber structures, wheels' parts, furniture and farm fittings
layout: a three-walled shed open to the light
bench by the door, rough timber under the eaves
saw pit in the floor for big beams
entries.found: beside the smithy in most villages, often sharing the yard
entries.notes: The general contractor of pre-industrial life: beams, doors, cart bodies, coffins. Wood shavings are the kindling that fires the village oven.

entries.name: Wheelwright's workshop
entries.purpose: building and repairing wooden cart and wagon wheels
layout: a wide shop with a turning bay and an assembly bay
wheels hang from the rafters by stage of build
iron tyres heated for shrink fitting
entries.found: in coaching towns and big market villages
entries.notes: A wheel that does not wobble at speed kills the horse before it kills the driver. The tyranny of the round was the wheelwright's whole trade.

entries.name: Cooper's workshop
entries.purpose: making and repairing barrels, casks and buckets for drink and dry goods
layout: a long shed with a toasting fire at one end
staves seasoning under the eaves
finished casks rolled to the door
entries.found: in brewing towns, ports and anywhere wine and ale move in casks
entries.notes: The barrel was the shipping container of the pre-modern world: beer, wine, oil, nails, gunpowder. Cooper details survive in every whisky distillery today.

entries.name: Potter's workshop
entries.purpose: making storage jars, cookware and roof tiles from local clay
layout: a shed for throwing next to a bigger kiln shed
greenware dries on racks before firing
kiln fired once a week, smoke all day
entries.found: where clay is good and wood is cheap, often near the brickworks
entries.notes: Roof tiles and storage jars made a town. The workshop smells of wet earth; the kiln firing is a two-day communal event when the whole village keeps the fire.

entries.name: Field brickworks
entries.purpose: making bricks for building and paving
layout: a long clay pit with the shed and kiln beside it
bricks moulded, stacked to dry for weeks, then fired in a clamp
clamp drawn after a week's slow burn
entries.found: wherever clay beds are worked, often a seasonal operation
entries.notes: A clamp kiln is bricks stacked as fuel among bricks: the outer layers fire the inner. Whole towns rose on bricks fired a few miles away in a single summer.

entries.name: Weaver's cottage
entries.purpose: cottage-industry handloom weaving of cloth for merchants
layout: a long upper room with tall windows for light
looms in a row, one worker each
yarn and finished cloth below or in the garret
entries.found: in clusters of cottages in woollen-cloth districts
entries.notes: A whole economy lived in the garret: the merchant left wool and collected cloth, paying by the piece. Deafening, dusty, and the crack of the loom carried down the lane.

entries.name: Tannery
entries.purpose: turning raw hides into leather by tanning with oak bark
layout: a series of stone vats dug in the yard by a stream
hides move down the line from beam to lime to tan
tanned hides dried on frames or hung in the loft
entries.found: on the downwind edge of towns and villages, never upwind
entries.notes: The stink was the trade's address: bark tannin and lime. A hide took months in the pit; the tanner's yard was unmistakable from three fields away.

entries.name: Oil press house
entries.purpose: crushing olives or other oil seeds into oil for food, light and medicine
layout: a vaulted stone room with a millstone basin at the centre
crushed paste in baskets under the press beam
oil runs into settling jars against the wall
entries.found: in every olive-growing district, one per estate
entries.notes: The beam press is a machine older than the plough: a tree trunk on a pivot, weighted with stone. Pressing was collective; the whole village brought its olives in November.

entries.name: Skep apiary
entries.purpose: keeping bees for honey and wax for candles and church wax
layout: skeps set in a row on stands or in a sunny wall bank
entrance holes face away from the house
heather or clover within flight range
entries.found: in cottage gardens and monastery walls
entries.notes: Bee boles — recesses in a south-facing wall holding skeps — are still visible in old monasteries and estate walls. Honey was the only sweet before sugar; wax lit every church.

entries.name: Chandler's workshop
entries.purpose: making tallow and wax candles for light
layout: a long shed with a rendering copper at the back
wicks on racks dipped in succession
finished candles hung from the poles to cool
entries.found: in market towns, near the tallow-chandler's raw materials supply
entries.notes: The ancestor of the light bulb and the chemical plant: rendering tallow is unglamorous chemistry. Smell was the signature — fat and smoke and nothing else.

entries.name: Dovecote
entries.purpose: keeping pigeons for meat (squabs) and guano fertiliser
layout: a squat tower or a raised loft on the barn gable
nesting boxes inside from floor to eaves
entrance above human reach but below the eaves
entries.found: on manor farms and estates; in North Africa, entire villages share a dove tower
entries.notes: Squabs were high-status meat and guano was black gold for the garden. A right to keep a dovecote was a seigniorial privilege in medieval Europe.

entries.name: Dogon banco granary
entries.purpose: storing millet and sorghum above the damp, termite-proof and rodent-proof
layout: a squat cylinder standing on stones in the family compound
carved shutter door high up, reached by a notched log ladder
grain above, family goods below
entries.found: in clusters around every Dogon family compound in Mali's Bandiagara region
entries.notes: The male granary (guyo ana) is the compound's bank vault; the carved door shutter records the owner's lineage. Raised on stone against termites and damp.

entries.name: Takakura raised rice storehouse
entries.purpose: storing rice and valuables dry and above rats
parts: raised floor on posts 2-3 m up
layout: a small timber box on tall posts
floor high above ground, discs blocking rat ascent
entrance by ladder which is drawn up after use
entries.found: rebuilt as heritage at Yayoi sites such as Yoshinogari and Karako-Kagi; rural form survives as kura storehouses
entries.notes: The raised silhouette that gave birth to the Shinto shrine's shinmei-zukuri style. Rat guards on every post are the signature; capstones and crossed finials echo the roof.

entries.name: Qullqa
entries.purpose: imperial storage of food, textiles, tools and weapons for redistribution and the army
layout: a small one-room box on a hillside, in rows of hundreds
two ventilation levels drive air through and keep food frozen and dry
door deliberately tiny to limit thieves and cold loss
entries.found: in vast rows near imperial roads and provincial centres, e.g. the 27-qullqa complex at Ollantaytambo
entries.notes: Storage on an imperial scale: the Mantaro Valley alone held 2,573 catalogued qullqas storing an estimated 170,000 square metres of goods. Cheap hillside, fierce wind, freezing nights — a freezer built before refrigeration.
